---
title: "Why can both X / Y and Y / X average more than 1?"
date: 2026-09-24
draft: true
categories:
  - statistics
  - r
---

Following up on [the ratio of normal variables](../../../2023/05/is-the-ratio-of-normal-variables-normal/index.qmd): if two independent variables have the same mean, must their ratio average to 1? Let's try both directions, using the same pairs of observations.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(20260924)
n <- 1000000
mu <- 1
sigma <- 0.2
X <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
Y <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

summarize_ratios <- function(x, y) {
  data.frame(
    pairs = length(x),
    mean_X = mean(x),
    mean_Y = mean(y),
    ratio_of_means = mean(x) / mean(y),
    mean_X_over_Y = mean(x / y),
    mean_Y_over_X = mean(y / x)
  )
}

knitr::kable(summarize_ratios(X, Y), digits = 4)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


| pairs| mean_X| mean_Y| ratio_of_means| mean_X_over_Y| mean_Y_over_X|
|-----:|------:|------:|--------------:|-------------:|-------------:|
| 1e+06| 0.9999|      1|         0.9999|        1.0461|        1.0463|


:::
:::


Both sample averages of ratios are above 1, although the ratio of sample means is close to 1.

One correction to the earlier post: for these independent, untruncated normals, the population ratio mean is actually **undefined**, not the ratio of the means. A normal denominator can land arbitrarily close to zero; a stable-looking simulation does not fix the [absence of finite moments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.14306).

To make the expectation argument valid, keep only pairs for which **both** values lie between 0.2 and 1.8. These are now independent truncated normals, still with population means exactly 1 by symmetry, and bounded away from zero. Truncating only at zero would not suffice.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lower <- 0.2
upper <- 2 * mu - lower
keep <- X >= lower & X <= upper & Y >= lower & Y <= upper
x <- X[keep]
y <- Y[keep]

knitr::kable(summarize_ratios(x, y), digits = 4)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|  pairs| mean_X| mean_Y| ratio_of_means| mean_X_over_Y| mean_Y_over_X|
|------:|------:|------:|--------------:|-------------:|-------------:|
| 999870| 0.9999|      1|         0.9999|        1.0459|        1.0462|


:::
:::


[Jensen's inequality](https://pages.stat.wisc.edu/~shao/stat609/stat609-06.pdf) says that for a convex function, $E[f(Y)] \geq f(E[Y])$. The reciprocal $f(y)=1/y$ is strictly convex for $y>0$: downward fluctuations increase the reciprocal more than equally sized upward fluctuations decrease it. Here, for example, $1/0.8=1.25$, whereas $1/1.2\approx0.833$.

For our truncated variables, independence and strict convexity give

$$
E[X/Y] = E[X]E[1/Y] > \frac{E[X]}{E[Y]} = 1,
\qquad
E[Y/X] = E[Y]E[1/X] > \frac{E[Y]}{E[X]} = 1.
$$

The inequality is strict because each denominator varies. Since $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution, the two expectations are equal. Let's compare their running averages with the common expectation, calculated by numerical integration.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mass <- pnorm(upper, mu, sigma) - pnorm(lower, mu, sigma)
expected_ratio <- mu * integrate(
  function(z) dnorm(z, mu, sigma) / (z * mass),
  lower = lower, upper = upper
)$value

k <- unique(round(exp(seq(log(100), log(length(x)), length.out = 300))))
running <- cbind(cumsum(x / y)[k] / k, cumsum(y / x)[k] / k)
matplot(
  k, running, type = "l", log = "x", lty = c(1, 2),
  col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(1, expected_ratio, running),
  xlab = "Number of retained pairs", ylab = "Running average"
)
abline(h = 1, col = "grey60", lty = 3)
abline(h = expected_ratio, col = "black", lty = 3)
legend(
  "bottomright",
  legend = c("X / Y", "Y / X", sprintf("Expectation: %.4f", expected_ratio), "1"),
  col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "black", "grey60"),
  lty = c(1, 2, 3, 3), bty = "n"
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Both running averages approach the same expectation above 1 for the truncated normals.](index_files/figure-html/fig-running-ratio-means-1.png){#fig-running-ratio-means fig-alt='Running averages of X / Y and Y / X plotted against sample size, with reference lines at 1 and their shared theoretical expectation.' width=672}
:::
:::


There is no contradiction: the average of reciprocals is not the reciprocal of the average.
